title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about reflection: what it means to reflect at university, and how to do it. By the end you will be able to explain what reflection is and why it matters, describe a simple model for reflecting, and recognise what keeps a reflection honest and balanced.

Reflection is not an add-on. 'Reflect on your learning' is one of the most common things you will be asked to do, in coursework, on placements, and in professional life. Knowing what it really involves, and having a model and the honesty to use it, turns a vague instruction into a habit that drives your development.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what reflection is and why it matters at university
describe the stages of a simple reflective model
identify what makes a piece of reflection honest and balanced.

title: In real academic practice
body: Reflection is the habit that turns experience into learning. Every assignment you review, every placement or project you look back on, every time you ask why something went as it did, draws on the same skill. Build it now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the professional practice that expects you to keep learning from what you do.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what reflection is and why it matters. Second, a simple model for reflecting: describe, reflect, take action. Third, how to keep a reflection honest and balanced. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

title: Orientation
body: You have probably been told to 'reflect' on a task, or to keep a reflective log, without being sure what that really involves. Reflection is not just writing down what happened. It is a deliberate, honest look back at an experience so that you can learn from it. This lesson is about what reflection is and why it matters, so the instruction to reflect stops being vague and starts being something you can actually do.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and reflection may be new as something to do on purpose. At this stage you are not expected to produce polished reflective essays. The aim is to recognise reflection when you see it and understand why it matters - the foundation you will build on as you progress.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that reflection is a deliberate, honest looking-back, not just a description of what happened
recognise reflective thinking in a worked example of a student looking back on a piece of work
identify why reflection matters for your development as a learner in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Reflection is a deliberate, honest look back at something you have done, so that you can learn from it and do better next time. It is more than remembering what happened: it asks what the experience was like, why it went the way it did, and what you would change.

This matters because at university you are expected to become a self-regulating learner: someone who takes charge of their own progress rather than waiting to be told how they did. Reflection is the engine of that progress. It is how experience turns into improvement, in your studies now and in professional life later. This lesson is about what reflection is; the lessons that follow give you a simple model for doing it and show you how to keep it honest.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent piece of work you got back. Did you look back at it, or just note the mark and move on? What is one question you could ask yourself about it now?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Reflection at university is a deliberate, honest look back at your experience so you can learn from it - not just a description of what happened, and not only for things that went wrong. You can now explain what reflection is, recognise it in how a student looks back on their work, and say why it matters: it is how a self-regulating learner turns experience into improvement. The next lesson gives you a simple model for doing it.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that reflection is a deliberate look back that helps you learn. But a blank page is hard to start from. This lesson gives you a simple model, three stages to move through, so that reflecting becomes a process you can follow rather than a vague instruction.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to master a complex reflective framework yet. The aim here is to learn one straightforward model, understand what each of its three stages asks, and see how they fit together.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the three stages of a simple reflective model: describe, reflect, take action
give an example of what happens at each stage
match a reflective statement about {{context}} to the stage of the model it belongs to.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A simple and widely used model breaks reflection into three stages. First, describe: give a brief, honest account of what happened. Second, reflect: assess the experience, that is, what went well, what did not, and why. Third, take action: decide what you will do differently as a result, so the reflection leads to a real improvement.

The three stages matter because each does a different job, and skipping one leaves the reflection incomplete. Describing without reflecting is just a record. Reflecting without taking action is a thought that changes nothing. The model keeps all three together, so looking back actually feeds into what you do next.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of something you did recently for your course. Try the three stages on it in your head: what happened, why, and what you would change. Which stage was hardest to do?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A simple reflective model has three stages: describe what happened, reflect on why and what you make of it, and take action by deciding what to do differently. You can now describe the three stages, give an example of each, and recognise which stage a reflective statement belongs to. Keeping all three together is what turns looking back into moving forward. The next lesson looks at what keeps a reflection honest and balanced.

title: Orientation
body: You now know what reflection is and have a simple model for doing it. But a model only helps if you are honest when you use it. This lesson is about what keeps reflection genuine: looking at the good as well as the bad, and being truthful with yourself rather than defensive or harsh.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to write a searching personal analysis. The aim here is to notice the difference between a balanced, honest reflection and a one-sided one, and to see what tips a reflection into being genuinely useful.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain why honest reflection looks at what went well as well as what did not
tell a balanced reflection apart from a one-sided one
identify what makes a reflection about {{context}} honest rather than defensive or purely self-critical.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A reflection is only useful if it is honest and balanced. Honest means telling yourself the truth about why something went as it did, rather than making excuses or blaming circumstances. Balanced means looking at the positives first, even when the negatives feel louder: no piece of reflection should be entirely positive or entirely negative.

This matters because a one-sided reflection teaches you little. If you only list faults, you miss what is worth keeping and you can end up discouraged rather than improved. If you only praise yourself, you never find what to change. Honest balance is what lets reflection do its job: it shows you both what works, so you can repeat it, and what does not, so you can fix it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you usually talk to yourself after something goes wrong. Are you more likely to make excuses, or to be too hard on yourself? What would a balanced, honest version sound like?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A reflection is only useful when it is honest and balanced: looking at the positives first, never landing all on one side, and being truthful about your own part without being harsh. You can now explain why balance matters, tell a balanced reflection from a one-sided one, and recognise what makes a reflection honest rather than defensive or self-critical. With what reflection is, a simple model for doing it, and the honesty to use it well, you are ready to reflect on purpose.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Reflection is no longer a vague instruction: it is something you can describe and begin to do. You can explain what reflection is - a deliberate, honest look back that helps you learn - and why it matters for your development. You have a simple model to follow: describe, reflect, take action. And you know what keeps a reflection honest and balanced: looking at the positives first, never landing all on one side, and being truthful without being harsh. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, reflection is something you practise across your studies and beyond. Each piece of work you review, each placement or project you look back on, each honest account of what you would change, is the habit at work. It is also what professional life expects: the ability to learn from experience, deliberately and honestly, travels well beyond your degree.

body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced reflective practice courses take reflection into structured cycles, turning it into sustained action and into a professional practice you own. title: Explore the concept
body: Four common ideas about what reflection is. Turn each card to see past the misunderstanding.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: Reflection is not simply retelling what happened. A description stops at the events; reflection asks why they happened as they did and what you make of them. The facts are the starting point, not the destination.

front.title: Not only when it goes wrong

back.body: Reflection is not just for mistakes. Looking honestly at what went well matters just as much, because you learn as much from understanding a success as from fixing a failure.
Reflection is not a box ticked at the end of a module. It is a habit you bring to your learning again and again, a regular looking-back that keeps feeding into what you do next.
Reflection is not performed to please a tutor. Its purpose is your growth as a learner: it is how a self-regulating student turns each piece of experience into the next improvement.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students who have just had the same essay returned with a middling mark and some feedback.

{{learner-a}} reads the feedback, notes that the mark was lower than hoped, and writes in the reflective log: 'I got 58. The tutor said my argument was unclear and I lost marks on referencing. I will try harder next time.' This records what happened and ends with a vague intention. It is a description, not a reflection: it does not ask why the argument was unclear or what 'trying harder' would actually involve.

{{learner-b}} reads the same feedback and looks back honestly. 'My argument was unclear because I started writing before I had decided what I actually thought, so each paragraph pulled a different way. The referencing slipped because I left it to the last night. Next time I will write a one-sentence position before I draft, and add each reference as I use the source.' This is reflection: it asks why things went as they did and turns that into specific, doable changes.

Both students looked back at the same essay. Only {{learner-b}} moved past describing it to learning from it.

title: Making a look-back a reflection
body: These habits turn a look-back into a genuine reflection. Try them on your next piece of returned work.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I described what actually happened, briefly and honestly?
Have I asked why it went the way it did, rather than just what the result was?
Have I looked at what went well, not only what went wrong?
Have I been honest with myself, rather than blaming or excusing?
Have I named something specific I would do differently?
Have I treated this as something to learn from, not a box to tick?

title: Explore the concept
body: The three stages of the model, one at a time. Open each to see what it asks.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Stage 1: Describe
_items.body: Start with a short, honest account of what happened. Stick to the facts: what you did, what the task was, how it turned out. Keep it brief, because the description sets the scene, it is not the reflection itself. The aim is a fair record you can then think about.

_items.title: Stage 2: Reflect
_items.body: Now assess the experience. What went well? What did not go as planned, and why? This is the heart of the model: you move from what happened to why it happened and what you make of it. Look at the positives as well as the negatives, and be honest with yourself.

_items.title: Stage 3: Take action
_items.body: Turn the reflection into a plan. Based on what you have noticed, what will you do differently next time? The action should be specific enough to act on. This stage is what makes reflection worthwhile: it is where looking back becomes moving forward.

_items.title: How the stages fit together
_items.body: The three stages run in order, each feeding the next: you describe so you have something to reflect on, you reflect so you know what to change, and you take action so the reflection makes a difference. Miss a stage and the chain breaks.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students use the three-stage model to reflect on the same group presentation that did not go well.

{{learner-a}} writes: 'The presentation was rushed and we ran over time. It was stressful. I hope the next one goes better.' This describes the experience and names a feeling, but it stops there. It offers no real reflection on why it was rushed, and the 'hope' is not an action. Two of the three stages are missing.

{{learner-b}} works through all three. Describe: 'We ran over time and had to cut the last section.' Reflect: 'We ran over because we never rehearsed with a timer, and we had split the slides without agreeing who said what, so we overlapped. The research itself was strong.' Take action: 'Next time we will rehearse once against a clock and agree who speaks to each slide beforehand.' This is the full model: a fair description, an honest assessment of good and bad, and a specific action.

Both reflected on the same event. Only {{learner-b}} moved through all three stages, so only {{learner-b}} came away with something to do differently.

title: Working through the three stages
body: Use these questions to check you have moved through all three stages of the model.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Describe: have I given a brief, honest account of what actually happened?
Reflect: have I asked why it went the way it did?
Reflect: have I looked at what went well as well as what did not?
Take action: have I decided on something specific to do differently?
Is my action concrete enough that I could actually do it next time?
Have I moved through all three stages, rather than stopping at the description?

title: Explore the concept
body: Four things that keep a reflection honest and balanced. Select each tab to read about it.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that idea.

_items.title: Look at the positives first
_items.body: Even when a piece of work went badly, start with what went well; you can almost always find something. Looking at the positives first keeps the reflection fair and stops it becoming a list of faults, and it tells you what is worth holding on to.

_items.title: Never all positive or all negative
_items.body: No honest reflection is entirely positive or entirely negative. A glowing account hides what could improve; a wholly negative one hides what is working. Real experiences are mixed, and a truthful reflection says so.

_items.title: Be honest, not defensive
_items.body: It is tempting to explain away a poor result by blaming bad luck, the question, or other people. Honest reflection owns your part in what happened. That is not about being hard on yourself, it is about looking at the things you can actually change.

_items.title: Honest, not harsh
_items.body: Honesty cuts both ways. Being unfairly hard on yourself is as distorting as making excuses. A good reflection is truthful and fair: it names what went wrong without turning the whole thing into a verdict on you as a person.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students reflect on the same seminar in which their presentation of a reading fell flat.

{{learner-a}} writes only the negatives: 'I was terrible. I froze, I rushed, the whole thing was a disaster and everyone could tell. I am just not good at this.' This is honest about the difficulty, but it is one-sided and harsh. It names no positives, turns a single seminar into a verdict on the student as a person, and offers nothing to build on.

{{learner-b}} reflects on the same seminar in balance: 'The start was shaky and I rushed when I lost my place. But I had understood the reading well, and the point I made about the author's assumption landed, because two people picked it up. I froze mainly because I was reading from dense notes. Next time I will use short prompts instead.' This looks at the positives first, is honest about the difficulty without being cruel, and finds something to change.

Both found the seminar hard. Only {{learner-b}} reflected in a way that was honest, balanced, and actually useful.

title: Keeping a reflection honest and balanced
body: Use these questions to keep your reflection honest and balanced.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I started with what went well, before the negatives?
Is there at least one positive and one thing to improve, rather than all one way?
Have I been honest about my own part, rather than blaming circumstances?
Have I avoided being unfairly harsh on myself?
Have I described this experience, rather than passing a verdict on myself as a person?
Would someone reading this learn both what worked and what to change?

title: Formative check: what reflection is
displayTitle: Which of these best describes what reflection is?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best describes what reflection is?

_items.text: A deliberate, honest look back at an experience in order to learn from it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflection looks back in order to learn, not simply to record.

_items.text: A written record of exactly what happened, step by step.
_items.feedback: That is a description; reflection goes further and asks why and what to change.

_items.text: Something you do only when a piece of work goes badly.
_items.feedback: Reflection is for successes too, not only for things that went wrong.

_items.text: A task you complete to show a tutor you finished the work.
_items.feedback: Reflection is for your own learning, not to prove completion.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflection is a deliberate, honest look back in order to learn.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about looking back in order to learn.
_incorrect.final: Reflection is a deliberate, honest look back in order to learn. The other options mistake it for a plain record, a response to failure, or a box to tick.

title: Formative check: recognising reflection
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's log a reflection rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's log a reflection?

_items.text: They asked why things went as they did and turned it into specific changes.
_items.feedback: Yes. Asking why and planning specific changes is what makes it a reflection.

_items.text: They recorded the mark and the feedback accurately.
_items.feedback: Recording accurately is description; reflection asks why and what to change.

_items.text: They wrote more than the first student.
_items.feedback: Length is not what makes a reflection; asking why and planning change does.

_items.text: They promised to try harder next time.
_items.feedback: A vague promise to try harder is not a reflection; a specific change is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student asked why and turned it into specific changes.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID beyond recording the feedback.
_incorrect.final: The second student reflected because they asked why things went as they did and planned specific changes, not because they recorded accurately or wrote more.

title: Formative check: why reflection matters
displayTitle: Why does reflection matter for your development as a learner in {{context}}?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does reflection matter for your development?

_items.text: It is how you turn experience into improvement, taking charge of your own progress.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, reflection is how experience becomes improvement.

_items.text: It fills space in a reflective log so the module is complete.
_items.feedback: Filling a log is not the point; learning from experience is.

_items.text: It proves to your tutor that you worked hard on the task.
_items.feedback: Reflection is for your own learning, not to prove effort.

_items.text: It lets you record your marks so you can look them up later.
_items.feedback: Recording marks is not reflection; learning from the experience is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, reflection turns experience into improvement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about turning experience into improvement.
_incorrect.final: Reflection matters in {{context}} because it turns experience into improvement and puts you in charge of your progress, not because it fills a log or proves effort.

title: Formative check: the three stages
displayTitle: The three stages of the simple reflective model, in order, are:
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What are the three stages of the model, in order?

_items.text: Describe, reflect, take action.
_items.feedback: Yes. Describe what happened, reflect on why, then take action.

_items.text: Plan, do, review.
_items.feedback: That is a different cycle; this model is describe, reflect, take action.

_items.text: Reflect, describe, conclude.
_items.feedback: The order starts with describing, then reflecting, then taking action.

_items.text: Describe, explain, repeat.
_items.feedback: The third stage is taking action, not repeating.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The model is describe, reflect, take action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which set names describing, assessing, then acting?
_incorrect.final: The model has three stages in order: describe, reflect, take action. The other options rename or reorder them.

title: Formative check: naming the stage
displayTitle: In the worked example, which part of the second student's reflection is the 'take action' stage?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which part is the take action stage?

_items.text: Deciding to rehearse against a clock and agree who speaks to each slide.
_items.feedback: Yes. Deciding what to do differently is the take action stage.

_items.text: Stating that the group ran over time and cut the last section.
_items.feedback: That is the describe stage: an account of what happened.

_items.text: Explaining that they overlapped because roles were not agreed.
_items.feedback: That is the reflect stage: working out why it happened.

_items.text: Noting that the research itself was strong.
_items.feedback: That is part of reflecting: assessing what went well.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding what to do differently is the take action stage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which part says what the student will do differently next time?
_incorrect.final: The take action stage is deciding to rehearse against a clock and agree roles. Stating what happened is describe; working out why is reflect.

title: Formative check: matching the stage
displayTitle: You are reflecting on a task in {{context}} and you write: 'I think it went wrong because I left the reading too late.' Which stage of the model is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which stage is 'it went wrong because I left the reading too late'?

_items.text: Reflect, because you are assessing why it happened.
_items.feedback: Yes. Working out why is the reflect stage.

_items.text: Describe, because you are giving an account of what happened.
_items.feedback: Describing is just the facts; here you are asking why, which is reflecting.

_items.text: Take action, because you are deciding what to do differently.
_items.feedback: No action is named yet; you are still working out why.

_items.text: None, because this does not belong to the model.
_items.feedback: Asking why something happened is exactly the reflect stage.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Asking why it went wrong is the reflect stage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Is the student describing, working out why, or deciding what to change?
_incorrect.final: Working out why the task went wrong is the reflect stage. Describing is just the facts, and taking action names a specific change.

title: Formative check: why balance matters
displayTitle: Why should an honest reflection look at what went well, not only what went wrong?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why look at what went well, not only what went wrong?

_items.text: Because you learn what is worth repeating, not only what to fix.
_items.feedback: Yes. Positives show you what to keep doing, as well as what to change.

_items.text: Because tutors prefer reflections that sound positive.
_items.feedback: Balance is for your learning, not to please a tutor.

_items.text: Because negatives are not a real part of reflection.
_items.feedback: Negatives matter too; the point is to include both.

_items.text: Because a longer reflection always earns a higher mark.
_items.feedback: Length is not the point; honest balance is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Looking at the positives shows you what is worth repeating.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What do you gain by noticing what went well?
_incorrect.final: An honest reflection looks at the positives so you learn what to repeat, not only what to fix. It is not about pleasing a tutor or writing more.

title: Formative check: balanced versus one-sided
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reflection more balanced than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second reflection more balanced?

_items.text: It named what went well and what went badly, honestly and without being harsh.
_items.feedback: Yes. Naming both sides, fairly, is what makes it balanced.

_items.text: It was more negative about the student's own ability.
_items.feedback: Being more negative is one-sided, not balanced.

_items.text: It avoided mentioning anything that went wrong.
_items.feedback: Ignoring the negatives is just as one-sided as ignoring the positives.

_items.text: It was shorter and stuck to the facts.
_items.feedback: Sticking to the facts is description; balance means weighing good and bad.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Naming both what went well and what went badly, fairly, makes it balanced.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A balanced reflection includes both sides; which option does that?
_incorrect.final: The second reflection was balanced because it named the good and the bad honestly and fairly. Being more negative, or ignoring the negatives, is one-sided.

title: Formative check: honest, not defensive
displayTitle: You are reflecting on a task in {{context}} that went poorly. Which response is honest rather than defensive?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response is honest rather than defensive?

_items.text: Owning the part you played in how it went, while noting what you did well.
_items.feedback: Yes. Owning your part, while being fair to yourself, is honest reflection.

_items.text: Putting the poor result down entirely to bad luck and an unfair task.
_items.feedback: Blaming circumstances entirely is defensive, not honest.

_items.text: Deciding you are simply no good at {{context}} and leaving it there.
_items.feedback: That is harsh and one-sided, not honest and balanced.

_items.text: Recording only the positives so the reflection reads well.
_items.feedback: Recording only the positives is one-sided and avoids the honest part.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Owning your part, while noting what you did well, is honest reflection.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Honest reflection owns your part without being harsh or defensive.
_incorrect.final: An honest reflection in {{context}} owns your own part while staying fair to yourself. Blaming bad luck is defensive, and writing yourself off is harsh.

body: What is the best description of reflection at university?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best description of reflection?

_items.text: A deliberate, honest look back at an experience in order to learn from it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflection looks back in order to learn.

_items.text: A written record of exactly what you did, in order.
_items.feedback: That is a description, not a reflection.

_items.text: A task you do only when something has gone wrong.
_items.feedback: Reflection is for successes too.

_items.text: A note of your mark so you can look it up later.
_items.feedback: Recording a mark is not reflection.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflection is a deliberate, honest look back in order to learn.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what reflection is really for.

body: Why does reflection matter for you as a learner?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does reflection matter for you as a learner?

_items.text: It is how you turn experience into improvement and take charge of your own progress.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflection turns experience into improvement.

_items.text: It proves to your tutor that you completed the work.
_items.feedback: Reflection is for your own learning, not proof of completion.

_items.text: It fills the reflective log the module requires.
_items.feedback: Filling a log is not the point of reflection.

_items.text: It guarantees a higher mark on the next assignment.
_items.feedback: Reflection helps you improve, but it guarantees nothing on its own.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflection turns experience into improvement and puts you in charge of your progress.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what reflection does for your development.

body: What are the three stages of the simple reflective model, in order?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What are the three stages of the model, in order?

_items.text: Describe, reflect, take action.
_items.feedback: Yes. Describe, then reflect, then take action.

_items.text: Plan, do, review.
_items.feedback: That is a different cycle.

_items.text: Describe, repeat, conclude.
_items.feedback: The stages are describe, reflect, take action.

_items.text: Reflect, describe, act.
_items.feedback: The order begins with describing.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The model is describe, reflect, take action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which set names describing, assessing, then acting?

body: A student writes: 'Next time I will add each reference as I use the source.' Which stage of the model is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which stage is 'next time I will add each reference as I use the source'?

_items.text: Take action.
_items.feedback: Yes. Deciding what to do differently is the take action stage.

_items.text: Describe.
_items.feedback: Describing is an account of what happened.

_items.text: Reflect.
_items.feedback: Reflecting is working out why something happened.

_items.text: None of the stages.
_items.feedback: Deciding what to do differently is exactly the take action stage.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding what to do differently is the take action stage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Is the student describing, reflecting, or deciding what to change?

body: What makes a reflection balanced?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes a reflection balanced?

_items.text: It looks at what went well as well as what went badly.
_items.feedback: Yes. Balance means including both sides.

_items.text: It lists only the things that went wrong.
_items.feedback: That is one-sided, not balanced.

_items.text: It focuses only on the positives.
_items.feedback: That is also one-sided.

_items.text: It is as long and detailed as possible.
_items.feedback: Length is not balance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A balanced reflection looks at both what went well and what went badly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A balanced reflection includes both sides.

body: Which of these is an honest reflection rather than a defensive one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is an honest reflection rather than a defensive one?

_items.text: Owning your own part in how something went, while noting what you did well.
_items.feedback: Yes. Owning your part, fairly, is honest reflection.

_items.text: Blaming a poor result entirely on bad luck.
_items.feedback: Blaming circumstances entirely is defensive.

_items.text: Deciding you are simply not capable and stopping there.
_items.feedback: That is harsh and one-sided, not honest.

_items.text: Recording only the positives so it reads well.
_items.feedback: That avoids the honest part.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Owning your part, while being fair to yourself, is honest reflection.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Honest reflection owns your part without being defensive or harsh.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what reflection is and why it matters, a simple model for doing it, and what keeps a reflection honest and balanced. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a polished reflective routine. The aim is to see reflection as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it carries on past this course and into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: show how what reflection is, a simple model and honest balance fit together as one practice
recognise reflective practice at work in a student's ongoing study
plan one way you will keep reflecting on your {{context}} study beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Reflective practice is reflection made a habit. It is not a one-off task you do when asked, but a cycle you run again and again: looking back at an experience, asking honestly why it went as it did, and deciding what to change. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one habit.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, reflection becomes something you do across a whole module and beyond, not once at the end. A short, honest look back after each piece of work, with one change carried into the next, is worth more than a long reflection written only when it is asked for.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one habit in your studies you could reflect on more regularly, such as how you plan, read or revise. What would you look back on, and when in your week would you do it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Reflection is most useful when it becomes a continuing practice. You run the cycle, honestly and in balance, again and again: look back, ask why, change one thing, and carry it forward. The three ideas from this course are the parts of that single habit, and it is the habit, not any one reflection, that improves how you study.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The practice as one cycle
body: Reflection works as a continuing cycle, not a one-off. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Describe
_items.body: Describe briefly and honestly what happened in a piece of work, without judging it yet.

_items.title: Ask why
_items.body: Ask why it went the way it did, looking at what went well as much as what did not.

_items.title: Decide a change
_items.body: Decide one specific thing you will do differently next time. One change is enough.

_items.title: Carry forward
_items.body: Carry that change into your next piece of work, then look back again. The cycle keeps turning.

title: Worked example
body: Two students finish a module having had the same feedback on an early essay. One reads it, nods, and moves on. The other looks back honestly, notes that the argument wandered, and plans to outline first next time. Over the term, the second student’s work improves because reflection became a practice, not a one-off.

title: Working with the cycle
body: Use these to keep reflection turning as a habit, rather than treating each piece of work as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I look back on this piece of work, not just note the mark?
Did I ask why it went the way it did, not only what the result was?
Did I stay honest, rather than blaming or making excuses?
Did I look at what went well as well as what went wrong?
Did I carry one change into my next piece of work?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat reflection as a continuing practice rather than a one-off task?
body: Why is it more useful to treat reflection as a continuing practice rather than a one-off task?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat reflection as a continuing practice rather than a one-off task?

_items.text: Because each round feeds the next: an honest look back changes what you do, and what you do gives you something new to reflect on.
_items.feedback: Yes. Run as a habit, each round of reflection feeds the next, so the thinking pays off over time.

_items.text: Because reflecting once, in detail, is enough to fix how you study for good.
_items.feedback: A single reflection rarely changes a habit. Reflection works when it is repeated.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to look at what went wrong.
_items.feedback: Honest reflection does look at what went wrong. That is part of what makes it useful.

_items.text: Because a continuing practice takes less thought than reflecting once.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. A habit spreads the thinking out so it stays manageable.

_feedback.correct: That’s right. Run as a habit, each round of reflection feeds the next, so the thinking pays off across your studies.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by repeating reflection rather than doing it once.

displayTitle: A student finishes an essay, looks back honestly at what went well and what did not, decides to plan earlier next time, and does so. The next essay is stronger. What does this show about reflection?
body: A student finishes an essay, looks back honestly at what went well and what did not, decides to plan earlier next time, and does so. The next essay is stronger. What does this show about reflection?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student finishes an essay, looks back honestly at what went well and what did not, decides to plan earlier next time, and does so. The next essay is stronger. What does this show about reflection?

_items.text: That reflection works as a continuing practice: the honest look back led to a change that improved the next piece of work.
_items.feedback: Yes. The whole cycle ran: look back honestly, change one thing, carry it forward.

_items.text: That the first essay was marked too harshly.
_items.feedback: The point is not the mark. It is that reflection led to a change that helped.

_items.text: That reflection only works for students who are already doing well.
_items.feedback: Reflection helped this student improve, whatever their starting point.

_items.text: That planning earlier is the only thing that ever improves an essay.
_items.feedback: Planning earlier was this student’s change. The practice is the honest look back that found it.

_feedback.correct: That’s right. The honest look back led to one change, carried into the next piece of work. That is reflection as a practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what the student actually did across the two essays.

displayTitle: You want to use reflection to improve how you study {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats reflection as a continuing, honest practice?
body: You want to use reflection to improve how you study {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats reflection as a continuing, honest practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use reflection to improve how you study your subject this term. Which plan best treats reflection as a continuing, honest practice?

_items.text: After each piece of work, look back honestly at what went well and what did not, decide one change, and carry it into the next piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole cycle, honestly, again and again. That is reflection as a practice.

_items.text: Reflect in detail once, at the end of term, on everything at once.
_items.feedback: One reflection at the end cannot change work you have already handed in.

_items.text: Only reflect on the pieces that went badly, so you do not dwell on them.
_items.feedback: Honest reflection looks at what went well too, not only what went wrong.

_items.text: Note how you feel after each task, without deciding to change anything.
_items.feedback: Noticing how you feel is a start, but reflection needs a decision to change something.

_feedback.correct: That’s right. Looking back after each piece, deciding one change, and carrying it forward keeps reflection going as an honest practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps reflection honest and repeats it over time.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which description best fits reflection as a continuing practice?
body: Which description best fits reflection as a continuing practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which description best fits reflection as a continuing practice?

_items.text: Running the cycle again and again - look back honestly, change one thing, carry it forward.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Writing one long reflection at the end of a module.
_items.feedback: That is a one-off, not a continuing practice.

_items.text: Recording your feelings after each class without changing anything.
_items.feedback: Reflection needs a decision to change something.

_items.text: Only reviewing work that went badly.
_items.feedback: Honest reflection looks at what went well too.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student reflects honestly on an essay, decides to outline earlier next time, and does so - and the next essay is stronger. Which parts of reflective practice has the student used?
body: A student reflects honestly on an essay, decides to outline earlier next time, and does so - and the next essay is stronger. Which parts of reflective practice has the student used?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reflects honestly on an essay, decides to outline earlier next time, and does so - and the next essay is stronger. Which parts of reflective practice has the student used?

_items.text: The honest look back, a decided change, and carrying it into the next piece of work.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Only the mark on the first essay.
_items.feedback: The mark is not the practice; the honest look back and the change are.

_items.text: Avoiding the feedback to stay positive.
_items.feedback: The student used the look back, not avoided it.

_items.text: Reflecting once and never again.
_items.feedback: The student carried a change forward, which is the continuing part.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
